subsection: 6. Energy value and dietary fibre targets

notes.b: Every nutrient releases a set amount of energy per gram, so we can work out how much energy a food supplies from its nutrient content. Carbohydrate is the main energy nutrient in most diets, so you need its figure and how to use it.
points: Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ (3.75 kcal) per gram. Sugars and starch have the same energy value per gram, so a gram of sugar gives no more energy than a gram of starch.
For comparison, protein provides 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram, fat 37 kJ (9 kcal) per gram and alcohol 29 kJ (7 kcal) per gram. Fat gives more than twice the energy of carbohydrate for the same weight.
Fibre (non-starch polysaccharide) is not digested by human enzymes, so it contributes little usable energy. Say 'little', not 'none'.
To calculate the energy from a food, multiply the grams of carbohydrate by 16 to get kilojoules (kJ), or by 3.75 to get kilocalories (kcal).
Worked example: 30 g of sugar provides 30 × 16 = 480 kJ, or 30 × 3.75 = 112.5 kcal. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ), which is why the kcal figure is smaller.

Label point: the nutrition declaration on a food label states carbohydrate and, of which, sugars; fibre is an optional item. The energy figure is calculated by the manufacturer, so it may not match your own calculation exactly.

Settings, comparative study: compare two breakfast cereals, one with added sugar and one without, using the label's carbohydrate, sugar and energy per 100 g. Discuss which supplies more energy and which supplies more fibre.

Settings, activity comparison: work out the energy in a food such as a bar of chocolate and compare it with the time an activity such as walking or running takes to use it up. Use the energy values from the source given with the question.
notes.tip: For a calculation, use 16 kJ (3.75 kcal) per gram and do not mix in other values within the same answer. Write fibre as giving little usable energy, never zero.

notes.h: Contribution of carbohydrates to the average diet
notes.b: Carbohydrate, mostly as starch, is the main source of energy in most diets, and it should supply the largest share of the energy in the diet, with fat and protein supplying the rest. The kind of carbohydrate matters, because some carries other nutrients and some does not.
points: Healthy eating guidelines use the Healthy Ireland Food Pyramid (Department of Health and HSE, 2016). Its base shelf is vegetables, salad and fruit, and the second shelf up is wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.
The top shelf holds foods high in fat, sugar and salt. These are eaten in small amounts and not every day, so they should not be the main source of energy.
Choose wholemeal and wholegrain starchy foods, because they supply energy together with fibre, vitamins and minerals.
Foods with a lot of added sugar supply energy but few other nutrients, so they are described as energy-dense and nutrient-poor ('empty calories').
Replacing sugary foods and refined starchy foods with wholegrain starchy foods, fruit and vegetables raises the intake of fibre and nutrients without raising the energy intake.
notes.tip: If asked which shelf of the Food Pyramid holds starchy foods, answer the second shelf up, with vegetables, salad and fruit below it. For adjusting a diet, say what you would reduce (such as confectionery), what you would increase (such as fruit, nuts and wholegrain) and give a reason.

notes.h: Dietary fibre: EFSA recommendation and how to meet it
notes.b: Fibre is the part of plant foods that humans cannot digest, and adults are advised to eat a set amount each day. Many Irish adults do not reach it, so you should know the target and the everyday ways to meet it.
points: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recommends a daily intake of dietary fibre for adults of 25 g a day. This is its adequate intake, set in 2010 for normal bowel function.
Irish healthy eating guidance from the Department of Health and the HSE (the Healthy Ireland Food Pyramid) also advises eating wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetables every day.
Breakfast: choose a high-fibre cereal (look for at least 3 g of fibre per 100 g on the label), porridge, bran or wholegrain bread or toast. Check the fibre per 100 g when choosing cereals.

Choose wholegrain or wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholemeal pasta and brown flour in baking in place of white versions, because the fibre is in the outer part of the grain that white versions have lost.
Add pulses such as beans, lentils, peas and chickpeas to soups, stews and salads. Half a tin of beans gives about 7.5 g of fibre, and chickpeas, kidney beans and butter beans give about 10 g.
Add two tablespoons of seeds a day, such as sunflower, sesame, pumpkin and linseed, or bran or porridge oats, to cereal, yoghurt, bread and salads.

Eat vegetables at lunch and dinner, about a third of each meal; frozen vegetables are as good as fresh. Leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, and bake or boil potatoes in their jackets, since most of the fibre in a potato is in the skin.

Eat 2-3 pieces of fruit a day (a piece gives about 2 g of fibre), and snack on fresh fruit, dried fruit or a handful of nuts instead of biscuits or crisps. Increase fibre gradually and drink plenty of water, because fibre absorbs water.
notes.tip: For 'three ways to increase fibre', give each with a reason or example, such as bran in cereal, more fruit and vegetables with skins on, brown bread, pasta and rice, or seeds and nuts. The Higher Level version ties your strategies to the EFSA recommendation.

notes.b: Added sugar supplies energy with few other nutrients, so cutting it down is a main healthy eating target. Strategies fall into two groups: what you buy, and how you prepare and eat food.
points: Purchasing: read labels and ingredient lists, because added sugars appear under names such as sucrose, glucose syrup, fructose, honey, cane sugar, brown sugar, corn syrup and fruit juice concentrate.
Choose reduced-sugar, lower-sugar or no-added-sugar versions of drinks, jams, cereals and yoghurts, choose fruit canned in juice rather than syrup, and avoid sugar-coated cereals.
Front-of-pack colour (traffic-light) labelling, where used, shows at a glance whether a food is high, medium or low in sugars. It is voluntary, so not every product carries it.
Preparing: reduce the sugar in recipes and use spices, vanilla or ripe fruit for flavour. Pureed fruit, banana, dates or apple can sweeten recipes instead of sugar.
Do not add sugar to tea, coffee or breakfast cereals. Replace fizzy drinks with water, or with fruit juice diluted with sparkling water, which cuts the sugar per glass.

Eat whole fruit rather than fruit juice or smoothies. Juice contains little fibre, and the sugar in juices and smoothies is released from the fruit's cells so it counts as free sugar, whereas whole fruit keeps its fibre and fills you up.
Snacks and treats: limit sweets, biscuits, cakes, sweet sauces and sugary drinks, and keep fresh fruit, fruit or vegetable sticks, nuts and natural yoghurt as snacks instead.
notes.tip: In 'devise strategies' questions, give purchasing and preparing strategies separately, one or two points each, with at least one of each.

notes.b: A diet high in sugar causes harm in several ways, some directly on the teeth and others through the energy and nutrients the diet supplies. Each effect needs its reason to earn marks.
points: Tooth decay: bacteria in plaque (the sticky film on teeth) ferment sugar to produce acid, which dissolves the enamel of the teeth.
Weight gain and obesity: sugary foods are energy-dense and nutrient-poor, so regular intake adds to excess energy intake.
Type 2 diabetes: a diet high in sugar and energy is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which is linked to excess body weight.

Heart disease and high blood pressure: high sugar intake is associated with a higher risk of heart disease and raised blood pressure. High fructose intake has been linked with higher blood pressure, and refined carbohydrate with excess insulin that can raise LDL cholesterol.
Nutritional deficiency: foods high in sugar displace fruit, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods from the diet, so vitamins and minerals fall short.
Sugary foods are also low in fibre, so they do little for bowel health.
notes.tip: When asked to identify or assess effects of a high-sugar diet, pick obesity, tooth decay, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure or nutritional deficiency, and give a reason for each. Do not claim sugar causes hyperactivity.

notes.b: Artificial sweeteners give a sweet taste without the energy of sugar, or with less of it. They fall into two types, intense and bulk, and each has its uses and limits.
points: Intense sweeteners, such as aspartame and saccharin, are many times sweeter than sugar, so only tiny amounts are needed and they add almost no energy.
Bulk sweeteners, such as sorbitol, mannitol and xylitol, have a similar bulk to sugar and provide some energy, though less than sugar.
Uses in food manufacture: they sweeten and improve palatability, and they are used in low-calorie, sugar-free, slimming and reduced-sugar foods, soft drinks and confectionery.
Sorbitol and other bulk sweeteners act as humectants: they retain moisture and stop products drying out.
Bulk sweeteners are used where sugar's bulk is needed, as in confectionery and fudge. Xylitol and sorbitol do not cause tooth decay, so they are used to avoid it.
Sweeteners cannot replace all of sugar's functions: they do not provide the bulk, browning, preserving or bulk-texture roles of sugar.
Sweeteners are food additives with E numbers. Labels must say 'contains sweetener', and aspartame carries a warning for people with phenylketonuria.
Excess bulk sweeteners can have a laxative effect, so their labels carry a warning.
notes.tip: To classify sweeteners, name intense (aspartame, saccharin) and bulk (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol) with an example of each. For uses in manufacture, give sweetening, low-calorie and sugar-free products, humectant action and avoiding tooth decay.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of energy a food provides, measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal).
A unit of energy, commonly called a Calorie, equal to about 4.2 kilojoules.
The part of plant food made of non-starch polysaccharides that the human digestive system does not break down.
A plant polysaccharide, such as cellulose or pectin, that forms dietary fibre.
A sweetener that is many times sweeter than sugar and so is needed in very small amounts.
A sweetener, such as sorbitol, that has a similar bulk to sugar and provides some energy.
A substance that absorbs and holds moisture, keeping a food from drying out.
The Irish food guide that places vegetables, salad and fruit at its base as the foods to eat most of.

factCards.term: Energy values per gram of protein, carbohydrate, fat and alcohol
factCards.definition: Protein 17 kJ (4 kcal), carbohydrate 16 kJ (3.75 kcal), fat 37 kJ (9 kcal) and alcohol 29 kJ (7 kcal).

factCards.term: Four effects of high sugar intake
factCards.definition: Tooth decay, weight gain and obesity, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease.

factCards.term: Four strategies for reducing sugar when preparing food
factCards.definition: Reduce the sugar in recipes, use spices, vanilla or ripe fruit for flavour, avoid adding sugar to drinks and cereals, and use unsweetened fruit in desserts.

questions.prompt: Calculate the energy provided by 40 g of starch, giving your answer in kilojoules and in kilocalories, and show your working.
questions.model: Energy value of carbohydrate: 16 kJ per gram. 40 × 16 = 640 kJ. Energy value of carbohydrate in kilocalories: 3.75 kcal per gram. 40 × 3.75 = 150 kcal.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the average diet can be adjusted to meet the EFSA fibre recommendation and reduce sugar intake, and evaluate the effects of a diet high in sugar on health.
questions.model: Fibre: swap white bread, rice and pasta for wholegrain versions; eat fruit and vegetables with skins on; add pulses to soups, stews and salads; add seeds, bran or porridge oats to cereals; choose high-fibre breakfast cereals and check the fibre per 100 g on the label; snack on fruit or nuts. Sugar: read ingredient lists for added sugars under names such as sucrose, glucose syrup, honey and fruit juice concentrate; choose reduced-sugar drinks and cereals; replace fizzy drinks with water or diluted juice; eat whole fruit rather than juice; do not add sugar to tea, coffee or cereals; limit sweets, biscuits and cakes. Effects of high sugar: tooth decay from acid produced by plaque bacteria; weight gain and obesity from energy-dense foods; type 2 diabetes; heart disease and high blood pressure; displacement of fruit, vegetables and other nutrient-rich foods, leading to nutritional deficiency. Sweeteners may reduce sugar and energy intake but cannot replace sugar's bulk, browning or preserving action.
